prompt: Which of the course's tools does it never run, and why?
hint: One of them exists only for one operating system.

choices.text: Metabase, because it needs a paid licence
choices.why: Metabase is open source and runs on the student's own machine from lesson 3.

choices.text: Power BI Desktop, which runs only on Windows
choices.why: Right. Lesson 4 shows its formulas beside SQL that computes the same numbers, and says which of the two ran.

choices.text: Streamlit, which is only available as a hosted service
choices.why: Streamlit is a Python library installed with pip; lesson 5 runs it locally.

choices.text: PostgreSQL, whose versions differ too much between systems
choices.why: PostgreSQL 16 is the database every lesson runs on.

prompt: Why can a lesson state that the median order is R$ 95.80 and expect your database to agree?
hint: Think about how the rows were made.

choices.text: Because the platform loads the same database for every student
choices.why: The platform runs no database; you build it yourself.

choices.text: The script draws its random rows from a fixed seed
choices.why: Right. The same seed on the same PostgreSQL version produces the same rows, so every count and median matches.

choices.text: Because the data was copied from a real shop's export
choices.why: Lantern is invented and its data is generated.

choices.text: Because a median does not depend on which rows exist
choices.why: A median depends entirely on the rows; it matches only because the rows match.

prompt: Why does the lesson ask for 4 GB of memory for the virtual machine when PostgreSQL alone would live in 2 GB?

choices.text: Metabase, a Java program, arrives in lesson 3
choices.why: Right. The same machine will carry PostgreSQL, Metabase and Streamlit, and Metabase is the heavy one.

choices.text: Ubuntu Server refuses to install with less
choices.why: The lesson does not say that; the reason is what runs on the machine later.

choices.text: The data set is loaded entirely into memory whenever a query runs
choices.why: Lantern's tables are small; a database keeps them on disk and caches what it reads.

choices.text: SSH needs a gigabyte per open connection
choices.why: An SSH session costs a few megabytes.

prompt: Why does the course have you work over SSH from your own terminal instead of in the virtual machine's window?
hint: The first thing lesson 1 asks you to do with a long script.

choices.text: SSH makes queries run faster
choices.why: The query runs in the same server either way.

choices.text: The window cannot show more than 25 lines
choices.why: Not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: Pasting long text there fails
choices.why: Right. A terminal on your own computer pastes normally, and the same connection is how you reach the machine every day.

choices.text: PostgreSQL refuses connections from a local console
choices.why: It accepts them; `psql` in the window would work.

prompt: On VirtualBox, match each forwarded host port to the program inside the machine it reaches.
What does the online path, a hosted PostgreSQL, leave you without?

choices.text: Nothing; it covers the whole course at no cost
choices.why: It covers the database only, and its free tier is a company's offer that can change.

choices.text: Somewhere to run Metabase and Streamlit
choices.why: Right. A hosted database is one of the four programs; the other two still need a machine or a hosted plan of their own.

choices.text: The ability to write SQL at all, since hosted databases use their own language
choices.why: Hosted PostgreSQL is PostgreSQL and speaks the same SQL.

choices.text: The seed, because hosted services disable random numbers
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so; the generator is plain SQL.

prompt: An order was placed at 22:30 on a Tuesday in São Paulo. On a database left at UTC, which day does `ordered_at::date` give?
hint: São Paulo is three hours behind UTC.

choices.text: Wednesday
choices.why: Right. 22:30 at −03 is 01:30 UTC the next day, which is why the lesson sets the database's time zone to São Paulo.

choices.text: Tuesday
choices.why: That is the local day; in UTC the moment has already crossed midnight.

choices.text: Monday
choices.why: UTC is ahead of São Paulo, not behind it.

choices.text: It depends on the client's operating system
choices.why: The cast uses the session's time zone setting, which comes from the database here.

prompt: The first run of `lantern.sql` prints `NOTICE:  schema "shop" does not exist, skipping`. What should you do?

choices.text: Create the schema by hand and run the script again
choices.why: The script creates it on the next line.

choices.text: Nothing, if the table of five counts follows
choices.why: Right. The script drops what an earlier run left, and on the first run there is nothing to drop.

choices.text: Reinstall PostgreSQL, because the default schema is missing
choices.why: `shop` is the course's schema, not one PostgreSQL ships.

choices.text: Grant yourself superuser and retry
choices.why: A permission problem says `permission denied`, not `does not exist`.

prompt: You created a view in the shop's schema and then ran `lantern.sql` again. What happened to the view?

choices.text: It survived, because views are stored in the catalogue, outside any schema
choices.why: A view lives in a schema like a table does.

choices.text: It survived but now points at the old rows
choices.why: A view stores a query, not rows, and this one was removed.

choices.text: It was dropped with the schema, along with every table in it
choices.why: Right. `DROP SCHEMA ... CASCADE` removes everything inside; the two database settings survive because they belong to the database.

choices.text: The script stopped with an error, because a view already existed with that name in the schema
choices.why: `CASCADE` exists precisely so the drop does not stop.

prompt: The script ran, printed an `ERROR` on line 100 and no table of counts. What is the likeliest cause, and the fix?

choices.text: The paste lost lines; paste the whole block again and rerun
choices.why: Right. A truncated script runs until the broken statement, and rerunning is safe because it starts by dropping what the broken run left.

choices.text: The server ran out of disk halfway through the load; free some space and retry
choices.why: A full disk says so in words, and not as a syntax error on one line.

choices.text: Your role lacks permission; ask for superuser
choices.why: That would read `permission denied`.

choices.text: PostgreSQL 16 does not support the script; upgrade
choices.why: The script was recorded on PostgreSQL 16.

prompt: Match each message to what it means.

pairs.right: the server runs and has no role in your name
you are known; that database is not there
nothing listens on the forwarded port

prompt: The script ran to the end, but your `orders` count is 7,098 instead of 7,102. What should you check first?
hint: The rows come from a seeded generator.

choices.text: Whether four orders were refunded since the lesson was written
choices.why: Nothing changes the generated rows after the script runs; refunds are generated too.

choices.text: That the file matches the lesson's block and the server is version 16
choices.why: Right. Same script, same seed, same version gives the same rows; a changed line or another version moves every count.

choices.text: The machine's clock, because rows are generated up to today
choices.why: The script's dates are fixed, ending on 17 June 2026.

choices.text: Whether the time zone setting was applied before loading
choices.why: The time zone changes how timestamps print, not how many rows there are.

prompt: What is the grain of `order_lines`?

choices.text: One row per order
choices.why: That is `orders`.

choices.text: One row per customer per day, summing what they bought
choices.why: No table in the shop has that grain.

choices.text: One row per product inside an order
choices.why: Right. 11,362 lines across 7,102 orders; an order of three products has three lines.

choices.text: One row per unit sold, so two bags make two separate rows
choices.why: Units are in `quantity`; a line of two bags is one row.

prompt: From the lesson's counts, how many lines does an average order have? Two decimal places.
A colleague reports "11,362 orders" from `SELECT count(*) FROM order_lines`. What went wrong?

choices.text: Refunded orders were counted twice
choices.why: Refunds are a status on `orders`; they are not duplicated in lines.

choices.text: The count included the test account's orders as well as the real ones
choices.why: True but small: four orders cannot explain more than four thousand extra.

choices.text: The table counts products in orders, not orders
choices.why: Right. Counting orders means counting `orders`, or `count(DISTINCT order_id)` on the lines.

choices.text: `count(*)` counts NULL values twice
choices.why: `count(*)` counts rows, once each.

prompt: What percentage of Lantern's orders were refunded? One decimal place.
Why does the shop keep money as whole cents rather than as a decimal number of reais in floating point?

choices.text: Sums of floating-point fractions drift by fractions of a cent
choices.why: Right. Integer cents add exactly, and a finance team reconciling to the cent notices the difference.

choices.text: PostgreSQL cannot store a decimal number exactly in any of its column types
choices.why: It has `numeric`; the choice here is about exactness of sums.

choices.text: Whole cents take much less disk space than decimal reais do
choices.why: Size is not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: Brazilian law requires prices in cents
choices.why: No such rule is involved.

prompt: In the lesson's histogram the last row, `400`, has 470 orders while the row before has 121. What does that jump mean?
hint: What `width_bucket` does with values past its upper bound.

choices.text: Orders between R$ 400 and R$ 450 are suddenly popular
choices.why: The last row is not a R$ 50 band; it collects everything above the range.

choices.text: It collects every order of R$ 400 or more, and there is a whole group up there
choices.why: Right. The slope would fade out; a jump says a second population sits past the bands — the office orders.

choices.text: A rounding error in `repeat`
choices.why: `repeat` only draws the bar; the count is 470.

choices.text: The three mis-priced orders
choices.why: Three orders cannot make 470.

prompt: Most orders are small, a few are very large, and the histogram slopes down to the right. What is that shape called?

choices.text: Normal
choices.why: A normal distribution is symmetric around its middle.

choices.text: Uniform
choices.why: A uniform distribution has bars of equal height.

choices.text: Right-skewed
choices.why: Right. The tail stretches towards the large values.

choices.text: Left-skewed
choices.why: The tail is named by where it stretches, and here it stretches right.

prompt: Lantern's mean order is R$ 170.23 and its median R$ 95.80. What does the gap tell you?

choices.text: The data has an error that makes the mean wrong
choices.why: The mean is arithmetic done correctly; it is the wrong summary for this shape.

choices.text: A minority of large orders pulls the mean far above the typical one
choices.why: Right. Half the orders are below R$ 95.80; a campaign planned around R$ 170 targets a customer the shop barely has.

choices.text: Most orders are above R$ 170
choices.why: Half are below R$ 95.80, so most are well below R$ 170.

choices.text: The median ignores the refunded orders
choices.why: Both were computed over the same rows of `order_totals`.

prompt: The quartiles of order value are 4790, 9580 and 16865 cents. What is the interquartile range, in reais?
The value with half the rows below it and half above is the ___.
A report says Lantern's average order is R$ 170.23. Who is that number accurate for?
hint: Compare it with each segment's median.

choices.text: For home customers, who are most of the orders
choices.why: Their median is R$ 85.80, half the figure.

choices.text: For office customers, who pay the most
choices.why: Their median is R$ 456.25, far above it.

choices.text: For neither group
choices.why: Right. It mixes two populations and lands between them, describing no actual customer.

choices.text: For both, since it is their weighted average
choices.why: Being a weighted average is exactly why it describes neither.

prompt: Under Tukey's rule, where is the upper fence?

choices.text: Two standard deviations above the mean
choices.why: That is a different rule, and it is moved by the outliers it is meant to find.

choices.text: 1.5 IQR above the third quartile
choices.why: Right. For Lantern that is R$ 349.78.

choices.text: At the 99th percentile
choices.why: A percentile cut always flags 1% of rows whatever the data holds.

choices.text: Twice the median
choices.why: Not Tukey's rule.

prompt: Of the 591 orders above the fence, 428 are office orders. What percentage is that? Nearest whole number.
Most of the orders above the fence are office orders. What is the right response?

choices.text: Delete them, since the rule flagged them
choices.why: They are real orders; deleting them removes a third of the shop's revenue from the record.

choices.text: Cap them at the fence value
choices.why: That invents values no customer paid.

choices.text: Split the segments apart
choices.why: Right. Against other office orders they are ordinary; the rule was measuring a mixed population.

choices.text: Fix them at the source, like the price errors
choices.why: There is nothing to fix; nothing in them is wrong.

prompt: Orders 412, 415 and 431 each have one line priced exactly 100 times the product's price. What is that most likely to be?

choices.text: A conversion to cents applied to a value already in cents
choices.why: Right. A factor of exactly 100 is the signature, and the correct value can be computed.

choices.text: Office customers buying a hundred bags of the same coffee in one order
choices.why: Quantity is its own column, and these are home customers.

choices.text: A seasonal price rise
choices.why: No price rises by exactly 100 times for three lines.

choices.text: The shop's test account
choices.why: That account is customer 1, whose lines cost one cent.

prompt: You found the three mis-priced lines. Why not simply divide them by 100 inside your report's query?

choices.text: Division by 100 loses precision in integer cents
choices.why: These values divide exactly; precision is not the problem.

choices.text: Every other query on the table still reads the wrong value
choices.why: Right. A fix hidden in one query repairs one report; the error belongs at the source, reported with how many rows it touched.

choices.text: PostgreSQL forbids arithmetic on primary keys
choices.why: The price is not a key.

choices.text: The lines are refunds and should stay as they are
choices.why: Nothing says these orders were refunded.

prompt: Customer 1's orders are worth one to three cents. Why does the IQR rule not flag them?

choices.text: The rule only looks at office orders
choices.why: It looks at every value.

choices.text: The lower fence is negative, so nothing falls below it
choices.why: Right. Which is why the minimum is worth its own query: some bad rows are inside the fences.

choices.text: One-cent orders are rounded down to zero by the view and then skipped
choices.why: Integer cents are not rounded.

choices.text: Four orders are too few for the rule to count them as a group at all
choices.why: The rule judges each value, however few.

prompt: Match each finding to what the lesson says to do about it.

pairs.right: fix at the source and report the rows touched

pairs.left: office orders far above home ones
one real customer who spent R$ 9,000 once
pairs.right: keep it and report the median beside the mean

pairs.left: one-cent orders from the shop's own account
pairs.right: exclude, and say so beside the number

prompt: Why does `corr(discount_pct, gross_cents)` return `NULL` for office orders?

choices.text: Office orders have missing values in `gross_cents`
choices.why: Every order has lines, so every total exists.

choices.text: There are too few office orders
choices.why: 684 orders is plenty for a correlation.

choices.text: Every office order has the same 15% discount
choices.why: Right. A column that never varies cannot vary with anything, and the formula divides by its zero spread.

choices.text: `corr` does not accept integer columns
choices.why: It computed 0.271 on the same columns over all orders.

prompt: Over all orders, discount and order size correlate at 0.271. Inside the home segment, at −0.005. What explains it?

choices.text: Discounts make customers buy more, and offices simply use more coupons
choices.why: If they did, the relationship would show inside each segment, and it does not.

choices.text: Offices get 15% off and also buy in bulk
choices.why: Right. The segment is a confounder, and the overall correlation is the gap between two groups.

choices.text: Large orders cause the shop to grant discounts
choices.why: Then home orders with a discount would be larger, and they are not.

choices.text: The home correlation is wrong because of rounding
choices.why: −0.005 is a computed value over 6,418 orders.

prompt: A third variable that drives both of the two you measured is called a ___.
Without orders 412, 415 and 431 the overall correlation rises from 0.271 to 0.447. What should you take from that?

choices.text: The discount effect is stronger than first thought
choices.why: It is still the segment gap, now measured without three errors.

choices.text: Three rows of 7,102 cannot matter, so the change is a bug
choices.why: They can: a correlation is built on squared distances, and those three are enormous.

choices.text: Find errors before computing a correlation, since a few extreme rows move it
choices.why: Right. The same applies to a standard deviation or a regression.

choices.text: The mis-priced orders were office orders
choices.why: They belong to home customers.

prompt: Which are cautions the lesson gives about a correlation? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: It measures only a straight-line relationship
choices.why: Right. A curve can give an r near zero.

choices.text: A few extreme rows can move it
choices.why: Right. Three rows moved it from 0.271 to 0.447.

choices.text: It says nothing about which causes which
choices.why: Right. r is the same number in either direction.

choices.text: It cannot be computed in SQL
choices.why: PostgreSQL computes it with `corr`.

prompt: Two days since April 2025 have no orders: 24 April and 14 August 2025. Why does the lesson treat only one as a fault?

choices.text: 14 August was a public holiday
choices.why: The lesson's evidence is the surrounding days, not a calendar of holidays.

choices.text: Its neighbours held 5 to 15 sales each; the other's about three
choices.why: Right. A zero is plausible when a day holds three orders and not when it holds ten.

choices.text: 24 April was a Sunday
choices.why: It was a Thursday, like 14 August.

choices.text: April's data is older, so it came through a less reliable pipeline
choices.why: Age is not the lesson's argument.

prompt: June 2026 has 513 orders against 855 in May. Why is that not a drop?

choices.text: June always sells less coffee
choices.why: Nothing in the data says so.

choices.text: Refunds were removed from June
choices.why: Refunds are counted in every month alike.

choices.text: The data ends on 17 June
choices.why: Right. Half a month drawn as a whole one looks like a collapse.

choices.text: The missing day of August is counted in June
choices.why: Missing data is missing; it is not moved.

prompt: Over the period Mondays have 1,495 orders and Sundays 537. By what percentage do Mondays exceed Sundays? Nearest whole number.
How does the lesson suggest comparing one day's orders so the weekly pattern does not distort it?

choices.text: With the day before
choices.why: That compares Monday with Sunday, which measures the calendar.

choices.text: With the same weekday a week earlier
choices.why: Right. Both days carry the same weekly effect, so the difference is about the business.

choices.text: With the average of every day in the month around it
choices.why: The month mixes all weekdays, so a Monday always looks high against it.

choices.text: With the same calendar date a year earlier, to remove the season
choices.why: That date falls on a different weekday.

prompt: Put the questions of an exploratory analysis in the order the lesson asks them.
items: what is in each table, and its grain
what a normal value looks like
what the findings mean for each number
trap: Finding outliers before knowing the shape is the usual slip: far is only far relative to what is normal.

prompt: Half of the lesson's findings end in a decision about what a number should include. Why does that lead to lesson 2?

choices.text: Two analysts deciding differently get two correct, different revenues
choices.why: Right. Refunds, the test account, the partial month: each choice changes the number, so the meaning has to be agreed and written down.

choices.text: Because every finding must be fixed in the data before any query can run
choices.why: Some are fixed upstream; most are decisions, not repairs.

choices.text: Because lesson 2 deletes the faulty rows
choices.why: Nothing in the course deletes rows to tidy a number.

choices.text: Because a dashboard tool will make the decisions automatically
choices.why: A tool computes whatever definition it is given.
